sections.section_title: The Foundation -- Raised with Christ, Therefore Seek What Is Above
sections.summary: If the Colossians were raised with Christ, they are to seek the things above, where Christ is seated at God's right hand, and set their minds on things above rather than on things on earth. The ground: they died, and their life has been hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is their life is revealed, they also will be revealed with him in glory.
sections.relevance: The passage contains some of the strongest language of security in Colossians. Three elements lean toward permanence: (1) The identification of Christ as 'your life' (he zoe hymon) -- their existence, in its truest sense, is Christ himself. (2) The statement that their life 'has been hidden with Christ in God' (kekryptai syn to Christo en to theo) -- a double concealment in the safest possible location. (3) The promise that 'when Christ is revealed, you also will be revealed with him in glory' -- a future certainty expressed with the temporal hotan ('when,' not 'if'). The neutral reading notes that the hiddenness does not mean unreality but 'the present invisibility of a reality that will one day be made visible.' However, the passage also contains imperatives ('seek,' 'set your minds') that ground the ethical commands of vv.5-17, and the neutral reading explicitly states at the chapter's conclusion: 'The conditional of 1:23 continues to operate.' The indicative realities ground the imperatives but do not replace them. The passage leans permanent because its indicative declarations about the community's position (hidden with Christ in God, destined for glory) are among the most secure-sounding statements in the letter, but this must be read alongside the chapter's sustained imperative framework.
key_phrases: if then you were raised with Christ, seek the things above
you died, and your life has been hidden with Christ in God
when Christ who is your life is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory

sections.section_title: Putting to Death What Is Earthly and Putting Off the Old Self
sections.summary: The Colossians are commanded to put to death what is earthly: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed (which is idolatry). On account of these, the wrath of God is coming. They once walked in these things but must now put them all aside: anger, rage, malice, slander, abusive speech. They must not lie, having stripped off the old self with its practices and put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of its creator. In this new humanity, all former identity markers are dissolved: Christ is all and in all.
sections.relevance: The section's relevance centers on the relationship between indicative and imperative, and on the explicit mention of divine wrath. The paradox is noted by the neutral reading: 'you died' (indicative, v.3) therefore 'put to death' (imperative, v.5). The death with Christ was a completed event, but the putting to death of earthly things is an ongoing, active outworking. The vices listed are not mere undesirable habits; they are 'the behaviors that provoke the judicial wrath of God' (v.6). The neutral reading draws a direct line: 'This aligns with the letter's concern about the Colossians' final presentation before God (1:22) and the conditional that governs it (1:23).' The coming wrath is eschatological -- the stakes are not merely moral improvement but divine judgment. The new self is 'being renewed' (present passive, anakainoumenon) -- an ongoing process, not a completed state. The passage leans conditional because it implies that believers who persist in the behaviors that provoke divine wrath face consequences, and the transformation from old to new self requires active, ongoing participation that is not guaranteed.
key_phrases: put to death therefore what is earthly in you
on account of these the wrath of God is coming
you have put off the old self with its practices
the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of its creator
Christ is all, and in all

sections.section_title: The Garments of the New Community
sections.summary: As God's chosen, holy, and beloved people, the Colossians are to put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, bearing with one another and forgiving as the Lord forgave them. Above all, they are to put on love, the bond of perfection. The peace of Christ is to rule in their hearts; the word of Christ is to dwell richly among them in teaching, admonishing, and singing with thanksgiving. Everything they do is to be done in the name of the Lord Jesus with thanksgiving to God. The section primarily addresses community ethics and worship practice rather than the permanence or conditionality of the believer's standing before God.

sections.section_title: The Household -- Relationships Reordered by Christ
sections.summary: The household code addresses paired relationships: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters. Each instruction is grounded in the community's relationship to the Lord. The extended instruction to slaves (3:22-25) emphasizes working heartily as for the Lord, with the promise that they will receive the inheritance as their reward from the Lord. The section closes with a warning: the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong done, and there is no partiality. The instruction to masters (4:1) grounds their treatment of slaves in the reality that they too have a Master in heaven.
sections.relevance: Two elements within this section directly touch the question of the believer's standing. First, the promise in 3:24: 'from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward.' The inheritance (kleronomia) -- the same concept from 1:12 ('the inheritance of the saints in light') -- is presented as something to be received in the future as a reward for faithful service to the Lord Christ. The framing as 'reward' (antapodosis) implies that the inheritance corresponds to conduct. Second, the warning in 3:25: 'the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.' The word prosopolempsia ('partiality') declares that God judges impartially -- whether slave or free, believer or not. The neutral reading notes: 'In a social system where masters could wrong their slaves with impunity, the declaration that there is no partiality with God would be heard as a leveling principle.' The passage leans conditional because it presents both positive consequences (inheritance for faithful service) and negative consequences (repayment for wrongdoing) based on conduct, with no exemption based on status.
key_phrases: from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward
you are serving the Lord Christ
the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done
knowing that you too have a Master in heaven
